extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in corporate governance, banking regulation, and consumer protection
extracted.subtask_description: A encyclopedic overview of the Wells Fargo cross-selling / fake-accounts scandal describing background, practices, regulatory responses, legal settlements, and long-term impacts. Useful for readers seeking a factual summary and timeline of the scandal and its consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-selling measurement (average products per customer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success by retail banks was measured in part by the average number of products held by a customer, and Wells Fargo was long considered the most successful cross-seller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references the 'Going for Gr‑Eight' initiative and frames cross‑selling as a core strategic metric (average products/customer) that drove employee behavior and management incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive sales quotas and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees faced intense pressure and extremely aggressive, sometimes 'mathematically impossible' quotas to produce sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include expectations as high as 20 products a day, bonuses for opening new accounts, and reports that unreachable goals led employees to open accounts without customer consent. The LA Times and other investigations documented these quotas as a principal driver of misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interagency Guidance on Sound Incentive Compensation Policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2010 NY DFS Interagency Guidance monitors incentive-based compensation structures and requires that banks appropriately balance risk and rewards, be compatible with effective controls and risk management, and be supported by effective corporate governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formal guidance is cited as the regulatory standard for designing incentive plans that do not encourage excessive risk-taking or unethical behavior; failure to align incentives with controls is implicated in the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on creating unauthorized accounts (consumer consent requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau fined Wells Fargo for the 'widespread illegal practice of secretly opening unauthorized accounts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening accounts without customer consent is characterized as illegal; enforcement remedies included fines, refunds, and mandated independent reviews. The page cites specific enforcement actions and dollar amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment tactics and anti-patterns indicating fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees used concealment tactics such as using their own contact information on applications, setting PINs to '0000', and ordering cards or services without customer knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational methods are described as concrete indicators of fraudulent account creation and enrollment in services; they illustrate how sales pressures translated into systemic misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower reporting and protections (effectiveness of ethics hotlines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of misconduct to supervisors or ethics hotlines often 'did not result in changes' or led to retaliation, including termination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights failures in internal reporting channels (e.g., Prudential whistle‑blowers were fired), implying that effective whistleblower protections and responsive ethics processes are essential governance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual arbitration clauses limiting consumer remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening of an account mandated customers enter into private arbitration with the bank, which limited customers' ability to pursue legal action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural/contractual feature functioned as a barrier to litigation for harmed consumers; the article uses it to explain how remedies were constrained prior to settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive accountability and compensation clawbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives faced hearings, resignations, forgoing of stock options, and clawbacks of compensation (e.g., $28 million recouped from John Stumpf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses these actions to demonstrate governance and board-level accountability mechanisms; clawbacks and enforced forfeitures are presented as remedial governance tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement and remedies (fines, oversight, restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators imposed fines and oversight (CFPB $100M portion, OCC $35M, state AGs, DOJ/SEC settlements), and the OCC added restrictions giving the bank oversight similar to troubled institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that regulatory agencies can (and did) impose monetary fines, settlement agreements, additional oversight, and even growth caps (by the Federal Reserve) as enforcement levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer remediation and settlement metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies included customer refunds, class-action settlements, and state attorney general settlements with quantified payouts (e.g., $6.1M refunds, $142M class action, $575M 50‑state settlement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scale of consumer restitution (number/amount of refunds, settlement sums) is used as an evaluative measure of the scandal's financial impact on consumers and company remediation efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace culture and employee welfare indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of employee experiences — frequent crying, stress leading to vomiting, panic attacks, and even consumption of hand sanitizer — are presented as indicators of a toxic sales culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employee wellbeing outcomes and reports of retaliation or damage to future employability (defamatory U5 filings) are used to assess internal cultural harm and the human cost of incentive structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational repair and business restructuring measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Post‑scandal actions included ad campaigns ('Re‑Established', 'This is Wells Fargo'), branch closures, divestitures (sale of student loan business, asset management), and cuts to consultant spending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures are framed as attempts to rehabilitate trust and alter business strategy; their effectiveness is discussed in media and analyst responses cited by the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance metric: 'cross‑sell ratio' and reliance on a 'sales organization'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'cross‑sell ratio' — how many accounts each customer had — served as an internal performance metric; Wells Fargo later discontinued branch-level sales quotas and said it would decrease reliance on its sales organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page points to this metric as central to managerial incentives and as an example of how metrics can drive harmful behavior when not balanced by controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal and client divestiture as external accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: States and cities (e.g., California, Chicago, Seattle) suspended or divested business relationships with Wells Fargo in response to the scandal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of public-sector business and municipal sanctions are presented as reputational and financial consequences and as a form of external pressure for corporate reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of investigations by multiple enforcement bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations were opened by various prosecutors, the Securities and Exchange Commission, state attorneys general, and congressional committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity of investigative venues (criminal, civil, securities, congressional oversight) is shown as a metric of severity and the range of legal/regulatory exposures a firm faces after systemic misconduct.
